title: ⭐⭐ Revision: the hours, the fence and the letter

questions.prompt: A pupil states his view in a letter and is told to justify it with a convincing argument. He has written: I do not think a course followed from home is any easier than one followed in a classroom. Which sentence justifies that view instead of merely repeating it?

options.text: I feel this very strongly, and nothing that anybody says will change my mind about it.
A course taken at home is, to my own mind, quite as demanding as one taken in a hall.
Most of the learners I know would say the same, and two of them have written about it.
The syllabus is the same, and the reading list is the same; only the room has changed.

questions.explanation: An argument hands the reader something he can go and check for himself, and this one does: the syllabus and the reading list named as unchanged, the room named as the one thing that did change, and a conclusion that follows from the pair. Whether those two really are the same is now open to inspection, which is exactly what makes it an argument rather than a declaration. Feeling something strongly adds volume and no evidence. Calling the course quite as demanding says the opening sentence again in different clothes and leaves the reader where he was. And a crowd is not a reason: how many people hold a view is a fact about the people, not about the view.

questions.prompt: Four sentences from a letter are each doing a different job in the argument. Match each sentence with the job it is doing.

options.text: In my view a course followed from home suits a working learner better.
I say so because the hours can be moved into the evening.
You are right that no timetable forces a learner to sit down.
The freedom that lets the work happen is the freedom that lets it stop.
granting a point to the other side
stating the opinion the letter defends
naming a drawback of the thing being discussed
giving the reason the opinion rests on

questions.explanation: Read each sentence for whose side it is on and what it is being used for. One announces where the writer stands and defends nothing yet; the words in my view are the giveaway. One begins on because and is therefore the support underneath it, naming the fact the opinion rests on. One is addressed to the other man and concedes something to him — the writer would not say you are right about a point he intended to attack. And one states a cost of the thing under discussion with no concession in it at all, which is what naming a drawback is. Notice how easily the concession and the drawback are swapped, since both turn on the same missing timetable: only one of them is addressed to the other man and handed to him as a point he has won.

questions.prompt: One sentence must carry both the jobs the comma is given in this lesson: fencing a phrase that explains the noun in front of it, and keeping the items of a list apart. Which sentence does both?

options.text: The evening class, a group of nine adults, meets on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday.
The evening class, a group of nine adults, meets in the small room behind the head's office.
The evening class meets on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday of every week.
The evening class meets on Monday, and it is a group of nine adults.

questions.explanation: Count the commas and ask what each one is doing rather than assuming they are all alike. The pair sitting on either side of the phrase that says what the evening class is fences an explanation; the single one further along keeps two of the three meeting days apart. Both jobs, one sentence. Where only a room is named there is no list to punctuate, and where no phrase explains the class there is nothing to fence. The line that simply joins two statements with and has a comma doing neither job: the fact about the nine adults has been left outside the sentence about the meeting days instead of being tucked into it.

questions.prompt: Four sentences make up one remark about the time an online course costs, and the remark works in one order only: each sentence answers the objection that the sentence before it has raised. Put them in that order.

options.text: One learner sleeps an hour less; another has stopped going to the match on Saturday.
But nobody has ever added a twenty-fifth hour to a day that already holds twenty-four.
Learning of this kind asks for hours, exactly as learning of every other kind does.
Yet a learner who has not got enough time can still make more of it.

questions.explanation: Follow the words that point backwards and the chain builds itself. Only one sentence opens the subject without leaning on anything before it, and it is the one that states the demand: hours are wanted here exactly as they are wanted anywhere else. That claim invites the obvious objection, and the sentence on but is the objection — a day cannot be lengthened. The sentence on yet answers it, and the yet is what fixes its place: a sentence that begins by conceding has to have something to concede to, so it cannot stand before the objection it is answering. The examples come last because they are the proof of that answer, not a new step: an hour of sleep and an hour of football are hours that were already going somewhere, sent somewhere else. Making time is never adding hours to a day; it is moving hours that a day already holds.

questions.prompt: A teacher tells the class to be tactful when they counter a point of view they have just granted to be valid. What does that instruction ask them to do?

options.text: to leave the point alone altogether and argue instead about some other matter
to disagree in language that spares the man the letter is addressed to
to drop the disagreement, a point once granted to be valid not being open to attack
to disagree only about the points they have not already granted to the other side

questions.explanation: Tact is about how a thing is said, never about whether it may be said. The instruction takes it for granted that you are going to disagree — it says when you counter, not if — and asks only that the wording spare the man on the other end of the letter. Every other reading turns a rule about manners into a rule about silence: giving up the disagreement leaves a letter with no view in it, and a point can be valid and still be answerable, which is the whole reason the word counter is in the sentence at all. Restricting the attack to points not yet granted avoids the difficulty by never entering it, and changing the subject abandons the reader in the middle of the argument he came for.

questions.prompt: Four statements are made about studying at a distance. Three of them name a benefit of it. Which one does not?

options.text: The journey to a classroom no longer has to be made twice on every school day.
A course may be followed from a town that has no college of its own.
The hours the course wants have still to be dug out of a week already full.
The hour at which the studying happens is the learner's own to choose, from dawn to midnight.

questions.explanation: Three of these hand the learner something: the hour is his, the place is his, and the daily journey has disappeared. The line about hours that must still be dug out hands him nothing — it tells him that the work itself has not shrunk and that those hours have to come out of a week that was already full. That is the drawback the whole page is built on, and it is easy to miss because it sounds so much like the others: it is a sentence about hours, in the same calm voice, and it is the only one of the four that costs the learner instead of paying him.
